title: Derivative bounds for a dilated smooth cutoff
statement: Use the real field [def-weil-field] and smooth functions in Euclidean coordinates [def-sfb-smooth-real-manifold]. Let $m\geq1$ and let $\theta:\mathbf R^m\to\mathbf R$ be smooth, equal to $0$ on $\{|\xi|\leq1\}$ and equal to $1$ on $\{|\xi|\geq2\}$. For $R\geq1$ put $\theta_R(\xi)=\theta(\xi/R)$. The function $\theta_R$ is smooth. For every $n\in\mathbf N$ there is a constant $A_n\geq1$, depending only on $n,m$ and $\theta$, such that for every multi-index $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\leq n$ and every $\xi\in\mathbf R^m$, $|\partial^\gamma\theta_R(\xi)|\leq A_n(1+R)^{-|\gamma|}$. For $\gamma=0$, $\theta_R(\xi)=0$ when $|\xi|\leq R$; for $|\gamma|>0$, $\partial^\gamma\theta_R(\xi)=0$ unless $R\leq|\xi|\leq2R$.

source.place: WANTED locally: Demailly, Differential and pseudodifferential operators on manifolds, §3.7, printed p.7 (PDF pp.7–8), equations in the cutoff proof immediately after the choice of θ; the scaled derivative estimate and annular support.

proof.text: Put $L_R(x)=R^{-1}x$, a continuous real-linear map since $R\geq1$. By [lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation], $\theta_R=\theta\circ L_R$ is smooth. The same node shows that each coordinate partial of a smooth function is smooth: compose its smooth differential with the continuous linear evaluation $T\mapsto T(e_j)$. For any ordered list $I$ of $k$ coordinate directions, prove $\partial_I(\theta\circ L_R)=R^{-k}(\partial_I\theta)\circ L_R$ by induction on $k$. The empty list is the identity. Given the formula for $I$, differentiate in direction $e_j$; the chain rule gives $D(\partial_I\theta)(L_Rx)[R^{-1}e_j]=R^{-1}\partial_j\partial_I\theta(L_Rx)$, and the constant factor $R^{-k}$ remains. This proves the formula for every list, hence for the fixed coordinate ordering defining every multi-index $\gamma$, with $k=|\gamma|$.

source.place: ContinuousLinearMap.contDiff and ContinuousLinearMap.iteratedFDeriv_comp_right, lines 161 and 461–467; agent coordinate induction from the real chain rule.

proof.text: If $|x|\leq R$, then $|x/R|\leq1$, so $\theta_R(x)=0$. On the open sets $|x|<R$ and $|x|>2R$, respectively, $\theta_R$ is identically $0$ and $1$. Every positive coordinate derivative vanishes there: the first derivative is zero by the difference quotient of a locally constant function, and induction applies because that derivative is identically zero on the same open set. Thus positive derivatives vanish outside $R\leq|x|\leq2R$. The same argument at $R=1$ gives vanishing of positive derivatives of $\theta$ outside the closed annulus $1\leq|x|\leq2$.

source.place: WANTED locally: §3.7 cutoff argument; agent proof directly from local difference quotients and the stated cutoff values.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-finite-dimensional-normed-proper] to $\mathbf R^m$ over the usual locally compact nontrivially normed field $\mathbf R$: the coordinate basis is finite, so $K=\{y:|y|\leq2\}$ is compact. By step 1 each $\partial^\gamma\theta$ is smooth, hence continuous. Apply [lem-sfb-compact-continuous-norm-bound] to each scalar-valued function $\partial^\gamma\theta$ on $K$ (target $\mathbf R^1$). There are finitely many $\gamma\in\mathbf N^m$ with $|\gamma|\leq n$, since each entry is at most $n$. Take $C_n$ to be the maximum of $1$ and their finitely many bounds. Off $K$, the order-zero function equals $1$, and every positive derivative is zero by step 2. Consequently $|\partial^\gamma\theta(y)|\leq C_n$ for all $y$ and $|\gamma|\leq n$, with $C_n$ depending only on $n,m,\theta$.

source.place: FiniteDimensional.proper, lines 553–556, and proper_real, lines 562–564; Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Group/Bounded.lean, IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn generated at lines 96–100.

proof.text: Set $A_n=2^n C_n\geq1$. For $k=|\gamma|\leq n$, steps 1 and 3 give $|\partial^\gamma\theta_R(x)|\leq C_nR^{-k}$. Since $R\geq1$, $(1+R)/R\leq2$, so $R^{-k}\leq2^k(1+R)^{-k}\leq2^n(1+R)^{-k}$. This is the required estimate, uniformly for all $R\geq1$. For $k=0$ this is simply the global bound for $\theta$, including when $n=0$. Together with smoothness and the support assertions in steps 1–2, it proves every clause.
